John Field
jon fēld
n. (John Field, c. 1545–1588, London preacher, co-author of the Admonition to the Parliament and organiser of the presbyterian movement)
Hebrew Yochanan, the LORD is gracious; Field, from Old English feld, open land.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

John Field was the organiser of the Elizabethan presbyterian movement and, with Thomas Wilcox, the author of An Admonition to the Parliament of 1572, the manifesto that first demanded of an English parliament the abolition of episcopacy and the establishment of presbyteries. Both men went to Newgate for it. Field was a London preacher, lecturer at Holy Trinity Minories, and above all a man of business: he kept the correspondence of the movement, collected the Register of its documents and of the sufferings of its ministers, organised the classes that met in secret through the 1580s, and coordinated the parliamentary campaigns. Whitgift's subscription drive silenced him repeatedly and he died in 1588, before the movement was broken. Hooker and his party dated the whole controversy from the Admonition, and they were right to. Field wanted a church ordered by the New Testament pattern and nothing else: “that thou shouldest set in order the things that are wanting, and ordain elders in every city” (Tit 1:5).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines an admonition as gentle reproof or counselling against a fault, and a classis as an assembly or convention of pastors.

expand to see more

ADMONI'TION, n. Gentle reproof; counselling against a fault; instruction in duties.

CLAS'SIS, n. In ecclesiastical affairs, an assembly or convention of pastors; a presbytery.

REG'ISTER, n. A written account or entry; a book of records.

Key Scripture

Tit 1:5 — "For this cause left I thee in Crete, that thou shouldest set in order the things that are wanting, and ordain elders in every city, as I had appointed thee:"

Act 14:23 — "And when they had ordained them elders in every church, and had prayed with fasting, they commended them to the Lord, on whom they believed."

Jer 6:16 — "Thus saith the LORD, Stand ye in the ways, and see, and ask for the old paths, where is the good way, and walk therein, and ye shall find rest for your souls. But they said, We will not walk therein."

Mat 15:9 — "But in vain they do worship me, teaching for doctrines the commandments of men."

Modern Corruption

The organiser of Elizabethan presbyterianism and co-author of the 1572 Admonition.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. Field is a useful corrective to the way reform movements are remembered. The names that survive are the writers and the martyrs; the man who kept the letters, built the register, arranged the meetings and timed the parliamentary bills is forgotten, and without him there would have been nothing for the writers to defend.

The principle to recover is that a church's order is something to be set right deliberately: “set in order the things that are wanting, and ordain elders in every city” (Tit 1:5). The old paths are to be asked for and then walked in (Jer 6:16), which takes organisation as well as conviction; and against the alternative stands the Lord's own verdict on worship built from men's commandments (Mat 15:9).

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek epidiorthoo (G1930), to set further in order; leipo (G3007), to be wanting; Hebrew nathib (H5410), a path.

Greek epidiorthoo (G1930) — to set further in order, correct; Titus 1:5.

Usage

"“set in order the things that are wanting” (Tit 1:5) — the Admonition of 1572."

"“when they had ordained them elders in every church” (Act 14:23) — the secret classes."

"“ask for the old paths, where is the good way” (Jer 6:16) — and then organise."
